```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Every stage of harnessr except one is a pure function of its input. Extraction,
cleaning, segmentation, ranking and merging give the same result every time.
The model call is the exception. It is the only step that costs money and the
only one that can die halfway through a long run. Above a temperature of zero,
it is also the only step whose reply can differ from one call to the next.

This guide covers how harnessr handles that step: the record each run keeps,
the limits every request is checked against before it is sent, a cache that
makes a repeat free, and a replay that reproduces a run from its trace with no
key and no spend. `vignette("harnessr")` introduces the package and its ideas.

## Setting up

The examples run offline. `hr_mock_client()` plays the part of the model, and
`embedder = "lexical"` gives free, deterministic word-overlap vectors in place of
an embeddings endpoint.

A mock costs nothing, so the spending limits below would have nothing to count.
The examples give it a price instead. `hr_register_model()` registers the model
id `"priced-mock"` at $2 per million input tokens and $8 per million output
tokens. Runs that name that model are priced at those rates, and most runs
below do.

```{r message = FALSE}
library(harnessr)

hr_register_model("priced-mock", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096,
                  input_usd = 2, output_usd = 8)
old <- hr_options(verbose = FALSE, embedder = "lexical")

cl <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.")
```

## What a run records

The answer carries everything in this section, and `print(ans)` sums it up:
the cost, where the evidence came from and, for a partial answer, why.

```{r}
ans <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "thorough",
                       client = cl, model = "priced-mock", max_tokens = 150)
ans
```

Check `ans$partial` first. `TRUE` means something degraded, and `ans$notes`
lists what: `dropped_chunks`, `failed_calls`, `unread_pages`, `call_cap_reached`,
`cost_cap_reached` and so on. `ans$warnings` holds every warning raised while the
document was read.

The trace holds every request the run made. `hr_trace_summary()` gives the
totals, `hr_trace_cost()` the bill by model, and `as.data.frame()` one row per
request with its stage, tokens, cost, time, prompt and reply:

```{r}
hr_trace_summary(ans$trace)[, c("calls", "cached", "tokens_in", "tokens_out", "errors")]
hr_trace_cost(ans$trace)[, c("model", "calls", "paid_calls", "usd")]
as.data.frame(ans$trace)[, c("step", "stage", "tokens_in", "tokens_out", "usd")]
```

The token totals measure the prompts and replies, so they show the size of a
run. The bill comes from `hr_trace_cost()`, which counts only the calls that
were issued. A call answered from a cache or a recording spent nothing, however
long its prompt. A model with no registered price contributes `NA`, never 0, so
no total can leave one out unnoticed.

`hr_estimate_cost()` prices a run before you make it:

```{r}
hr_estimate_cost("priced-mock", input_tokens = 120000, output_tokens = 4000)
```

### What each request records

Each request is one entry in `trace$steps`. Besides its label, prompt, reply and
the model requested, a step records:

- `params`, what the call asked for, and `params_sent`, the request as it went
  out with every default resolved: the model, `api`, `base_url`, the output cap
  sent, the temperature (`NA` when none was sent), the effort, the
  schema name, and SHA-256 hashes of the JSON schema and of any extra body
  fields. A small cap sent to a reasoning model is raised to 2048, and
  `params_sent` shows the raised cap.
- `served_model`, `response_id` and `fingerprint`, where the provider returns
  them. `model` keeps the model requested, and the step is priced and replayed
  by that model.
- `attempts`, the number of requests sent, retries included (0 for a reply from
  a cache or a recording), and `started_utc` and `ended_utc` in ISO 8601 UTC.
- `tokens`, with `provenance`: `"reported"` by the provider, `"counted"` here
  with the `"tiktoken"` tokenizer, or `"estimated"` with another one. Reasoning
  and cached input tokens the provider reports are kept as `tokens$reasoning`
  and `tokens$cached_input`, as parts of `output` and `input` rather than
  additions.

```{r}
step <- ans$trace$steps[[length(ans$trace$steps)]]
str(step[c("label", "attempts", "started_utc", "tokens")])
str(step$params_sent)
```

A mock reports no usage, so its counts are estimated. `hr_trace_summary()`
gives the share of requests whose counts were estimated as `usage_estimated`,
and `print()` on a trace reports that share when it is above zero.

`refine` and `hierarchical` also record the length of the state they carry
forward:

- Each `refine.draft` and `refine.revise` step has `state$tokens_in`, the length
  of the draft the request carried, and `state$tokens_out`, the length of the
  draft carried on from it (the old draft when the reply was unusable).
- Each `hier.summarise.L<k>` step has the length of the text it summarised and
  of the summary it returned.
- Each level adds a local `hier.state.L<k>` step with the number of summaries
  handed on and their combined length.

A draft that shrinks sharply in one revision shows up in these fields.

Each cut made to fit a limit writes a local `truncate` step. It holds where the
cut was made (`detail$where`), the token limit, and the tokens before, kept and
dropped. A `refine` or `hierarchical` answer also adds up the tokens cut in
`notes$tokens_truncated`, and printing the answer reports how many tokens were
cut to fit. Here a model with a 1,000-token window makes `refine` cut its
growing draft:

```{r}
hr_register_model("small-window", context_window = 1000, max_output = 500,
                  input_usd = 2, output_usd = 8)
long_draft <- paste(rep("Revenue was 45.2 million dollars, and the draft says so.", 30),
                    collapse = " ")
cut <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "fast",
                       client = hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) long_draft),
                       reader = "refine", model = "small-window",
                       max_tokens = 120, max_answer_tokens = 200)
cuts <- Filter(function(s) identical(s$label, "truncate"), cut$trace$steps)
str(cuts[[1]]$detail)
cut$notes$tokens_truncated
```

A cut can also be made at `refine.excerpt`, `hier.summaries`,
`preview.skim`, `preview.outline`, `<label>.input` for a finding cut to fit a
merge, `<label>.giveup` for the capped findings a failed merge returns,
`segment.contextual.header`, `segment.contextual.document`, `screen.opening`,
`synthesise.gaps` and `embed.input`.

A trace also records who the run is for and the settings it ran under.
`hr_trace()` takes `system`, `owner`, `run_by`, `purpose` and `approved_by`.
`hr_options(actor = list(...))` sets them for every trace, and a field you set
in neither place is `NA`. `trace$config` is a snapshot of the options in force
when the trace was made, plus the R version. It leaves out the values of
`api_headers`, since they can hold credentials.

```{r}
tr <- hr_trace(owner = "finance team", run_by = "ana", purpose = "Q3 check")
tr
names(tr$config)
```

`as_json(ans)` writes the answer with every prompt and response of its run.
`hr_trace_save()` writes the trace alone, and a replay reads that file.

### Errors and warnings by class

Errors are classed, so you can catch a specific failure:

- `gr_auth_error`, `gr_file_not_found`, `gr_empty_document`,
  `gr_unsupported_format`, `gr_overflow`, `gr_call_cap`, `gr_cost_cap`,
  `gr_budget_error`, `gr_unknown_model`, `gr_unknown_override`,
  `gr_no_recipes`, `gr_bad_ensemble` and `gr_missing_dep`.
- `gr_bad_setting` for a setting outside its choices (`vignette("extending")`).
- `hr_unknown_effort_key` and `hr_unpriced_model`, both covered below.
- `hr_dim_mismatch` when two vectors of different lengths are compared, such as
  a lexical fallback vector against an API embedding.

Degradations are classed warnings:

- `gr_segment_fallback`, `gr_embed_fallback`, `gr_rerank_degraded`,
  `gr_iterative_degraded`, `gr_ensemble_degenerate`, `gr_duplicate_recipe` and
  `gr_ocr_unavailable`.
- `gr_clamped` with `hr_param_clamped` for a parameter moved to its nearest
  bound (`vignette("extending")`).
- `gr_parallel_share` for a parallel item whose share refused a later request
  (below).
- `gr_bad_correct` for a `gr_compare()` `correct` function that fails (below).
- `gr_unclear_dropped` when `gr_extract()` leaves unclear screening records out
  (`vignette("review")`).

In an interactive session, a long read keeps one progress line up to date with
the number of chunks read and the spend so far. `gr_read_many()` also reports
the spend so far before each document.

## Limits

Two limits are on by default: a run may spend $5 and make 400 calls.

```{r}
unlist(hr_options()[c("max_cost_usd", "max_calls")])
```

They are checked at two points. The first is before the first request. A run
is refused there, with a classed error that names the option to change, when:

- it would need more calls than `max_calls`, or
- its reader sends every chunk, and sending them would already cost more than
  `max_cost_usd`.

Here `map_reduce` over five chunks needs six calls:

```{r}
chunks <- gr_segment(gr_example(), list(method = "sentence", max_tokens = 150))
spec <- gr_read_spec(reader = "map_reduce", model = "priced-mock")

tryCatch(
  gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue?", cl, spec,
          trace = hr_trace(governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 3))),
  gr_call_cap = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

### Every request is checked before it is sent

The second check runs on every request before it goes out. It compares the
limit with what the run has spent plus the most the request could cost: its
prompt at the input price and its output cap at the output price. The prompt
count includes the JSON schema and extra body fields the request carries and a
few tokens of framing per message, since the provider bills for all of that.
That count is then raised by `safety_margin`. A request that could take the run
past a limit is not sent, so a run ends at or under its limit rather than one
request over it.

Under a limit of one cent, the five chunk requests below go out and the merge
does not. The merge's reply cap is 1500 tokens, which at $8 per million could
cost more than the run has left, so the answer comes back partial:

```{r}
tr <- hr_trace(governor = hr_governor(max_cost_usd = 0.01))
capped <- gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue?", cl, spec, trace = tr)
capped$partial
data.frame(calls = tr$calls, spent_usd = tr$spent_usd, stop_reason = tr$stop_reason)
tr$refusals[[1]]$message
```

The bound assumes two things harnessr cannot see. The provider must stop each
reply at its cap, and its count of the prompt must fall within `safety_margin`
of the local tokenizer's.

A run that leaves its output caps at the model's limit stops while it still has
headroom that a smaller cap would have used. With the merge's reply held to 500
tokens, the same run fits:

```{r}
tr <- hr_trace(governor = hr_governor(max_cost_usd = 0.01))
fits <- gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue?", cl,
                gr_read_spec(reader = "map_reduce", model = "priced-mock",
                             max_answer_tokens = 500),
                trace = tr)
fits$partial
data.frame(calls = tr$calls, spent_usd = tr$spent_usd)
```

A refused request is not a call, and it adds nothing to the trace's calls, steps
or spend. `hr_call()` first signals a condition of class `hr_budget_refused`,
which you can catch to stop the run there. Otherwise it returns the request as a
failed result with `refused = TRUE` and an error naming the limit. The trace
lists the request in `refusals`, sets `budget_stop` and names the limit in
`stop_reason`: `"calls"`, `"cost"`, `"tokens"`, `"output"`, `"model"` or
`"unpriced"`. Readers and review stages mark the answer or section partial and
do not count the refused request as failed.

The check sits on the call path itself, so it covers every request: readers,
judges, the ensemble's adjudication, conflict resolution in `gr_extract()`,
context and proposition segmentation, claims, outlines, screening, synthesis,
embeddings, and any request a custom reader or a script makes with `hr_call()`.

### A governor for one run

`hr_governor()` holds a run's six limits. Attach one with
`hr_trace(governor = )`. A trace without a governor reads the limits from
`hr_options()` at each check.

| limit | what it holds | default |
|---|---|---|
| `max_calls` | requests the run may make, cache hits and embeddings included | 400 |
| `max_cost_usd` | what the run may spend, in USD | 5 |
| `max_tokens_total` | tokens of every prompt, reply and embedded text | off |
| `max_output_tokens` | the largest output cap one request may carry; a request with a larger one is refused, not cut down | off |
| `allowed_models` | the model ids the run may call, text and embedding models alike | any |
| `allow_unpriced` | whether a model with no registered price may be called under a spending limit | `FALSE` |

Each limit is also an option of the same name:
`hr_options(max_tokens_total = 50000)` sets it for every run, and each trace's
config snapshot lists all six. `NULL` or `Inf` removes a limit. A limit that
cannot be compared is refused as soon as you set it:

```{r}
tryCatch(hr_options(max_cost_usd = NA), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

A request to a model the run may not call is refused the same way as one over
budget:

```{r}
tr <- hr_trace(governor = hr_governor(allowed_models = "gpt-4o"))
res <- hr_call(cl, "What was revenue?", model = "priced-mock", trace = tr)
data.frame(refused = res$refused, stop_reason = tr$stop_reason)
```

`gr_read_many()`, `gr_claims()`, `gr_outline()` and `gr_synthesise()` keep a
trace of their own and fold it into the trace you pass them. Their requests are
held to that trace's governor, less what it has already spent and the tokens it
has used. `max_calls` stays a limit per document and per stage. `gr_compare()`
holds the whole comparison to `max_cost_usd` and `max_tokens_total`.

### Models with no price

A language model with no registered price adds nothing to the spend, so no
spending limit could stop it. While `max_cost_usd` is set, a request to such a
model is refused with a condition of class `hr_unpriced_model`, and `gr_read()`
stops before its first request. `hr_backend_client()` wraps an R function as a
paying client, which lets this example show the refusal offline:

```{r}
hr_register_model("unpriced-model", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096)
backend <- hr_backend_client(function(messages, params) "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.")

res <- hr_call(backend, "What was revenue?", model = "unpriced-model")
res$refused
res$error
```

Register the model's prices with `hr_register_model()`, or set
`hr_options(allow_unpriced = TRUE)`. Under `allow_unpriced`, its requests are
sent, still count against `max_calls` and `max_tokens_total`, and are priced
`NA` in the trace. `max_tokens_total` is then the limit that still bounds the
run. `hr_mock_client()` and replays are never refused for this, and neither are
embedding models with no price.

An `hr_ellmer_client()` is priced as the model its ellmer object was built with,
whatever a recipe names, so one built on a model with no registered price is
refused too. Register that model at your provider's current prices, or let a
local model run unpriced; `vignette("harnessr")` shows both.

Through ellmer, a `temperature` in a read spec is ignored with a warning,
because sampling parameters belong to the ellmer object. Embeddings come from a
function you pass as `embed =`. Without one, `retrieve` and the `semantic`
segmenter fall back to lexical vectors and warn.

### Parallel batches

With `parallel = TRUE`, per-chunk requests go out in batches that cannot be
stopped part way. The limits apply to them like this:

- Each worker's items are held to an equal share of the calls and dollars the
  run has left.
- An item that its worker's share refuses before it is sent runs again in the
  calling process, against the run's own limits.
- A batch the run's limits cannot cover runs in the calling process instead of
  being split across workers.
- Batch items make one request each. An item that made more, and had a later
  one refused by its share, warns with class `gr_parallel_share`, and the run is
  not marked as stopped.

### How much the model reasons

`effort` sets how much a reasoning model reasons on each call, stage by stage.
`vignette("readers")` explains how effort is billed, which models it is sent
to, and the label each stage's calls carry.

In a review, the same vector goes to each stage. `gr_screen()` and
`gr_extract()` take it as a recipe override; `gr_claims()`, `gr_outline()` and
`gr_synthesise()` take it as an argument. With
`effort = c(extract = "low", synthesise = "high")`, the per-chunk extraction
stays cheap and the spending goes to the writing.

A name that matches no declared call stops with an error of class
`hr_unknown_effort_key` that lists the stems. A misspelt `c(extrac = "low")`
therefore cannot send every extraction at the provider's default unnoticed.
`?gr_read_spec` lists every label and suggests a profile: low for the many
per-chunk calls, high for the few that judge.

## Paying once

`hr_cache()` stores each successful response, keyed on the exact request. A
repeat is free and identical:

```{r}
cache  <- hr_cache(file.path(tempdir(), "harnessr-runs-cache"))
cached <- hr_cache_client(cl, cache)

first  <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "thorough",
                          client = cached, model = "priced-mock")
second <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "thorough",
                          client = cached, model = "priced-mock")

hr_trace_summary(second$trace)[, c("calls", "cached", "tokens_in")]
hr_trace_cost(second$trace)[, c("calls", "paid_calls", "usd")]
```

`cached` counts the calls answered from the cache rather than the network, so
`calls - cached` is what the run paid for. The token counts stay, since that is
how big the prompts were, but a run with `cached == calls` cost nothing, so do
not hand its totals to `hr_estimate_cost()` and call the result a bill.

The key covers everything that can change the reply: the messages, the model,
the resolved output cap, the temperature, the JSON schema, the API shape and the
base URL. It does not cover the API key, the headers, the timeout or the retry
policy, none of which the model sees. If a header changes which model answers,
give that client its own `base_url` or `model` so the cache can tell them apart.
Failures are never cached: a rate limit or a refusal is a property of the
moment, and storing one would make a blip permanent. Neither is a reply cut off
at its output cap, or a structured reply that does not fit its schema, so
running again asks again.

The default directory is under `tempdir()`, so a cache costs nothing and
vanishes with the session. For a long run, point it somewhere real and the run
becomes resumable. Restart after a crash and every completed call is already
paid for:

```{r eval = FALSE}
hr_options(cache_dir = tools::R_user_dir("harnessr", "cache"))
```

`hr_cache_stats()` reports entries, bytes, hits, misses and writes, and
`hr_cache_clear()` empties a cache. Set `write = FALSE` to run against a frozen
cache, or `read = FALSE` to refresh entries already stored.

### Repeated draws

At a temperature above zero a cache hit replays one sample instead of drawing a
new one. That is what makes a run reproducible, but it also means N identical
calls are one draw N times, and anything that compares them sees perfect
agreement. To keep N draws, give each call its own `draw_index`. Above 0 it is
part of the key, so draws 1 to N are N entries, and a rerun gets the same N
replies back in the same order:

```{r}
n <- 0
sampler <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) { n <<- n + 1; paste("draw", n) })
sampler <- hr_cache_client(sampler, hr_cache(file.path(tempdir(), "harnessr-runs-draws")))

vapply(1:3, function(k) hr_call(sampler, "Pick one.", draw_index = k)$text, "")
vapply(1:3, function(k) hr_call(sampler, "Pick one.", draw_index = k)$text, "")
```

The second line is answered from the cache. A call with the default
`draw_index = 0` keys as an ordinary call always has. Use a fresh directory, or
`read = FALSE`, when you want new replies for draws already stored.

### Older caches

Entries are keyed by a SHA-256 hash under `harnessr-cache-v3`. Entries written
under the old key (`readgpt-cache-v2`, by readgpt 0.6.0 and earlier builds of
harnessr) are still read for calls with no draw index. The first reply found
that way in a session warns once, with class `hr_legacy_key`, and
`hr_cache_stats()` counts them as `legacy_hits`. Old entries are never
rewritten, and `hr_cache_clear()` removes both. With
`tools::R_user_dir("harnessr", "cache")` set, entries readgpt kept in
`tools::R_user_dir("readgpt", "cache")` are read too, after it.

## Replaying a run

A trace records every prompt and every response. That makes it a complete
transcript of the only non-deterministic part of the pipeline, so a trace plus
the source document reproduces a run exactly, with no key and no spend:

```{r}
f <- file.path(tempdir(), "run.json")
hr_trace_save(first$trace, f)

replayed <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "thorough",
                            client = hr_replay_client(f), model = "priced-mock")
identical(replayed$answer, first$answer)
```

Ship the trace next to the paper and a reader reproduces the run instead of
paying to approximate it. A trace file is also a re-runnable bug report: it
records exactly what went wrong.

A reply is matched on the key `harnessr-replay-v2`: the prompt messages, the
model the call asked for, its effort, its temperature once the session default
is filled in, the output cap asked for and its JSON schema. Each step records it
as `replay_key`. A prompt with no recorded reply raises `gr_replay_miss` rather
than inventing an answer. A miss means the replay has diverged from the
recording, and a result that looks like the original but is not is worse than no
replay at all. When the prompt was recorded under other settings, the message
names the recorded temperature, cap or schema next to the ones asked for. Pass
`strict = FALSE` to run a partial recording anyway.

A replay that asks for more replies than were recorded is an error too, of class
`hr_replay_exhausted`. Draw k of a request is answered with the reply recorded
for that draw:

```{r}
tr <- hr_trace()
n <- 0
sampler <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) { n <<- n + 1; paste("draw", n) })
invisible(lapply(1:3, function(k) hr_call(sampler, "Pick one.", draw_index = k, trace = tr)))

rp <- hr_replay_client(tr)
vapply(1:3, function(k) hr_call(rp, "Pick one.", draw_index = k)$text, "")
tryCatch(hr_call(rp, "Pick one.", draw_index = 4),
         hr_replay_exhausted = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

`hr_replay_client(on_exhausted = "flag")` repeats the last recorded reply
instead, which is what every replay did before, and counts each repeat in
`$stats()$repeats`. A step recorded before `replay_key` existed is looked up by
the old key, `readgpt-replay-v1` (messages, model and effort only), with one
`hr_legacy_key` warning per recording in a session.

### Embeddings in a replay

A trace records each embeddings request and what it cost, but not the vectors
that came back. A replay reproduces a run's chunk ranking exactly only when the
recording used a deterministic embedder and the replay uses the same one. Both
conditions, not either: replaying an API-embedded run with a deterministic local
embedder would compute vectors the original never saw while looking exact.
Anything else warns (`gr_replay_no_embeddings`) and falls back to lexical
vectors. Those place semantic cuts and rank chunks differently, so a replay of a
run that used embeddings (the `needle` recipe, the `retrieve` and `iterative`
readers, the `semantic` segmenter) usually sends prompts the recording does not
hold. A strict replay then stops with `gr_replay_miss`, whose message names this
cause.

Record a run you intend to publish with `hr_options(embedder = "lexical")`, as
this guide does, or with your own embedder registered as `deterministic = TRUE`:

```{r}
run <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "needle",
                       client = cl, model = "priced-mock")
again <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "needle",
                         client = hr_replay_client(run$trace), model = "priced-mock")
identical(again$chunks_used, run$chunks_used)
```

### Limits in a replay

A saved trace says whether a limit cut the run short (`budget_stop`,
`stop_reason`), and a replay under the limits it was recorded with stops where
it stopped. Replayed calls count against `max_calls` as they did when recorded.
When the spending limit stopped the recorded run, each replayed call also counts
what it cost when recorded against `max_cost_usd`, in the trace's
`replayed_usd`, though nothing is spent; for any other run it counts nothing, so
a replay of an expensive run is not stopped by the replaying session's limit.
A replay under a higher limit that asks for a call past the recorded stop gets a
`gr_replay_miss` saying so.

Traces do not store the JSON schema a call requested, only a hash of it in the
step's key. In a recording made before `replay_key` existed, two calls that
differ only by schema, temperature or output cap share a reply.

## Comparing what recipes cost

`gr_compare()` runs several recipes over one document on one trace. Its
`summary` says what each recipe cost: `calls`, `tokens_in`, `tokens_out` and
`usd`, priced at each model's registered price, and `usd_estimated`, the share of
those dollars spent on requests whose token counts were estimated locally. Give
`correct`, strings a right answer contains or a function of each answer, and it
adds `correct` and `usd_per_correct`, the cost of a right answer:

```{r}
cmp <- gr_compare(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", c("fast", "precise", "thorough"),
                  client = cl, model = "priced-mock", correct = "45.2 million")
cmp$summary[, c("recipe", "reader", "calls", "usd", "usd_estimated",
                "correct", "usd_per_correct")]
```

`usd_per_correct` is `usd` for a right answer, `Inf` for a wrong one that cost
something, and `NA` when correctness is not known. A recipe a limit stopped
before it found anything is `NA`, not wrong. A recipe is charged for a
segmentation it shares with an earlier recipe, as it would be run alone, so the
column can add up to more than `hr_trace_cost(cmp$trace)`.

## Models, prices and token counts

`hr_models()` lists the context windows and prices harnessr knows, and
`hr_model_limits()` and `hr_model_info()` look one model up. Check them before
a long run: an unregistered model falls back to a conservative 128k window with
no price, so its cost shows as `NA` rather than a wrong figure.
`hr_register_model()` fixes that in one line, and its `cached_input_usd` prices
input the provider served from its prompt cache at its own rate. A model with no
cached rate prices cached input as other input.

```{r}
hr_register_model("priced-reasoner", context_window = 128000, max_output = 16000,
                  input_usd = 2, output_usd = 8, reasoning = TRUE)
hr_models()[hr_models()$id %in% c("priced-mock", "priced-reasoner"),
            c("id", "context_window", "reasoning", "input_usd_per_1m", "output_usd_per_1m")]
```

`hr_tokenizer()` says which counter is in use. The default, `"heuristic"`, needs
nothing installed. `hr_set_tokenizer("tiktoken")` switches to OpenAI's own
tokenizer where the reticulate package and Python's `tiktoken` are installed: it
counts in a model's encoding when one is given and otherwise, as the package's
budgets do, in the larger of `cl100k_base` and `o200k_base`. For a model that
is not OpenAI's it is an estimate. Without those packages it stops rather than
falling back, because a silent fallback would change every budget calculation.

`hr_budget()` does the context arithmetic for every request. It cannot return a
non-positive input budget; it raises an error that says what to change instead.
`?hr_options` documents every setting.

## Choosing the settings

Three walkthroughs cover the settings that hold a run in: the limits every run
has, the governor a benchmark or a batch shares, and effort that rises only
when a stage needs it. Each says what the
setting controls and what it trades off, the signs in your results that point
to changing it, where its default came from, and how to test a change.
`vignette("settings")` lists every option with its default.

### The global limits {#set-limits}

**What they control.** `max_cost_usd` and `max_calls` hold every run, and
`max_tokens_total`, `max_output_tokens`, `allowed_models` and `allow_unpriced`
hold it further when set (see "Limits" above). A limit that is too low ends
runs early, with partial answers; one that is too high lets a mistake, such as
a reader that sends every chunk of a long document at a small chunk size, cost
what it costs.

**Signs they need changing.** An answer with `partial = TRUE` and
`cost_cap_reached` or `call_cap_reached` in its notes, a trace whose
`stop_reason` is set, or an error of class `gr_call_cap` or `gr_cost_cap`
before the first request means a limit stopped the run. Raise it only after
checking that the run should cost that much: `hr_estimate_cost()` and
`gr_chunk_stats()` say so before anything is sent. A run that spends far less
than its limit, every time, can have the limit lowered to catch the run that
does not. A refusal with `stop_reason = "output"` means a request's output cap
was larger than `max_output_tokens` allows, and lowering the reader's caps
(`max_answer_tokens`, `max_chunk_tokens`) fits it.

**Where the defaults came from.** $5 and 400 calls are limits for one read,
chosen so a mistake costs little; they are choices, not measured values, and
`gr_settings_table("options")` declares no evidence for them. The others are
off by default, and `allow_unpriced = FALSE` because a limit that cannot see
what a request costs is not a limit.

**How to test them.** A limit belongs to the run, not to an arm, so what a
sweep can test is which settings fit under it. A reader's output caps decide
how much of the limit each request reserves, so sweep the merge's cap and hold
each arm's five runs to the same $0.02:

```{r}
qa <- gr_qa_reference(questions = c(revenue = "What was revenue in 2024?"),
                      documents = gr_example(), answers = list("45.2 million"),
                      split = "dev")
arms <- hr_sweep(gr_arm("thorough", list(method = "sentence", max_tokens = 150,
                                         overlap_tokens = 0, model = "priced-mock")),
                 list(max_answer_tokens = c(1500, 500)))
vapply(arms, function(arm) {
  b <- suppressWarnings(hr_benchmark(arm, qa, runs = 5, client = cl, split = "dev",
                                     scorer = gr_scorer_answer(),
                                     governor = hr_governor(max_cost_usd = 0.02)))
  c(stopped = sum(b$failure_kind %in% "budget_stop"), usd = sum(b$usd))
}, numeric(2))
```

With the merge's reply capped at 1500 tokens, 3 of the 5 runs were stopped
before their merge, since each merge reserves $0.012 of output; capped at 500,
all five finished within the same limit. `suppressWarnings()` hides the
`hr_budget_stopped` warning each benchmark gives; in your own runs, read it.

### The governor of a benchmark or a batch {#set-governor}

**What it controls.** `hr_governor()` holds limits for more than one run.
`hr_benchmark(governor = )` holds the whole benchmark to it, each run to what
the runs before it left; `gr_read_many()` and the review stages hold their
documents to the governor of the trace they are given. Sized too small, the
last arms or documents are refused; sized too large, a mistake in one arm
spends the budget meant for all of them.

**Signs it needs changing.** `hr_benchmark()` warns with class
`hr_budget_stopped`, naming how many runs were stopped and by which limit, and
the stopped runs have `failure_kind = "budget_stop"`. Arms late in the list
stopped more than early ones is the sign of a governor too small for the whole
benchmark rather than an arm that costs too much.

**Where the default came from.** `governor = NULL` takes the limits from
`hr_options()` when the benchmark starts, and those are set for one read (400
calls), while a benchmark of two arms on 300 items for 5 runs needs several
thousand. Size it for the benchmark: arms x items x runs x requests per run.

**How to test it.** Count the requests one run makes, multiply, and check how
much of the governor was used:

```{r}
per_run <- 6  # map_reduce over five chunks: five chunk requests and a merge
needed <- length(arms) * 1 * 5 * per_run
bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, qa, runs = 5, client = cl, split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer(),
                      governor = hr_governor(max_calls = needed, max_cost_usd = 1))
c(allowed = needed, used = attr(bench, "trace")$calls,
  stopped = sum(bench$failure_kind %in% "budget_stop"))
```

`vignette("compare")` sizes a governor this way for every benchmark it runs.

### Effort that rises when needed: `effort_mode` {#set-effort-mode}

**What it controls.** With `effort_mode = "escalate"` a read starts every
stage at its `effort` (`"low"` when `effort` is unset) and sends the next
stage at `"high"` when something went wrong in the one before: a cut, a
reply stopped at its output cap, a reply that is not the JSON asked for,
`NOT_IN_DOCUMENT` from every request of the stage, a quotation `iterative`
could not verify, or `ensemble` members that disagree. Effort changes only at
a stage boundary, at most once a read, and the stage after a raised one goes
back to the base effort. It trades the cost of reasoning at a high effort on
every request against the cost of a wrong answer where low effort was not
enough; a raise costs nothing but the raised stage's reasoning.

**Signs it needs changing.** A fixed `"high"` effort whose bill is mostly
reasoning on requests that a low effort answers as well; or answers at a
fixed `"low"` that come back cut off, unparsed or not found. The trace shows
each raise as an `"effort.escalate"` step, and `hr_effort_log()` says which
trigger fired and whether the raised stage fired it again.

**Where the default came from.** `"static"` sends the effort `effort` names,
as before the setting existed (`untested`). Nothing has compared escalation
with a fixed effort here; `hr_effort_check()` makes that comparison.

**How to test it.** Here `refine` reads the report with a stand-in reasoning
model that, at low effort, finds nothing in the first chunk, where `refine`
drafts its answer:

```{r}
hr_register_model("priced-reasoner", context_window = 128000, max_output = 8192,
                  input_usd = 1, output_usd = 4, reasoning = TRUE)
thinks <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  if (identical(params$effort, "low") &&
      startsWith(messages[[2]]$content, "<excerpts>")) {
    return("NOT_IN_DOCUMENT")
  }
  "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars."
})
efforts <- hr_sweep(function(effort) {
  gr_arm("thorough", list(method = "sentence", max_tokens = 150, overlap_tokens = 0,
                          model = "priced-reasoner", reader = "refine",
                          effort = if (effort != "escalate") effort,
                          effort_mode = if (effort == "escalate") "escalate" else "static"))
}, list(effort = c("low", "high", "escalate")))
eb <- hr_benchmark(efforts, qa, runs = 5, client = thinks, split = "dev",
                   scorer = gr_scorer_answer(),
                   governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 200, max_cost_usd = 1))
sent <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(eb)), function(i) {
  d <- as.data.frame(attr(eb, "traces")[[eb$ledger_id[i]]])
  d <- d[!is.na(d$effort), ]
  data.frame(arm = eb$arm[i], stage = d$stage, effort = d$effort)
}))
table(sent$arm, paste(sent$stage, sent$effort))
hr_effort_log(attr(eb, "traces")[[eb$ledger_id[eb$arm == "thorough:effort=escalate"][1]]])
```

At `"low"` every request went out low, and at `"high"` every one high. Under
`"escalate"` the draft went out low and found nothing, which raised the four
revisions after it to high, and the log says the raise resolved the trigger:
the revisions found the figure. Four of the five requests of each run went
out raised here, because the draft is one request; on a reader whose first
stage is many requests (`map_reduce`'s chunks), the raised stage is the
smaller share. `hr_effort_check()` reads a benchmark of such arms with the
non-inferiority test of `hr_report()`, which needs a reference with a test
split and enough items and runs for intervals, so it runs on your own:

```{r eval = FALSE}
chk <- hr_effort_check(bench, candidate = "thorough:effort=escalate", margin = 0.05)
chk$contrasts[, c("reference", "estimate", "lower", "verdict")]
chk$cost
```

Register the margin with `hr_register_contrasts()` before the benchmark runs
and pass it as `registration`; without one, the result is marked post hoc.

```{r include = FALSE}
hr_options(old)
```
